We counted seven helmets, including the yellow one, and the motion light stayed on for twenty-three seconds. I left the rack in place because the damp patch was behind it, and we could see enough from the aisle.

At the far end of the shed, Ren was wiping the pump handle with a cloth. He had written a note in German for his cousin, who was collecting a bicycle later, and he explained the two words when I asked. The note said “er ist heute nicht da,” meaning “he is not here today,” and “um sieben,” meaning “at seven o’clock,” referred to the collection time. Those words were part of the note, not pauses in what he was telling me. Ren said his cousin would come at seven if the bus arrived on time, and he had left the blue bicycle beside the window so it would not block the main aisle. I moved the floor brush away from its front wheel, but did not move the bicycle. The back tyre was flat, and the pump gauge showed no reading until Ren pressed the valve straight.

We also checked the notice board, where the monthly rota was pinned beneath a clear plastic sleeve. Three names had been crossed out in pencil, but the replacement names were written in the margin rather than on the rota itself. Leah said, “We should copy those over before Sunday, or people will think the evening shift is uncovered.” I asked whether she wanted me to edit the paper copy, and she said she would do it after checking with the two volunteers. The small envelope for replacement spoke reflectors was still taped to the lower corner. It held four reflectors and a handwritten price of two euros each; we did not open the envelope. One corner of the plastic sleeve had split, so Martin put a note on the supplies list for a new sleeve, size A4, and left the rota where it was.

In the middle aisle, we found a silver bell and a pair of damp gloves on the bench. The bell had a strip of masking tape around its clamp, with the words “for the green bike” written in black pen. Nobody present knew which green bike the note meant, because there are two: one with a child seat and one with a front basket. We put the bell in the labeled lost property tray and listed the gloves separately because they were not attached to anything. I nearly wrote that both items belonged to the same person, then stopped because there was no name or tag. The gloves were size medium and had a small tear on the left thumb. Joel took a photograph of the bench and the two green bicycles so the evening volunteers could compare them with the note.

Before we finished, Martin checked the side latch three times. It closed if he lifted the door slightly, but it caught on the frame when he let the door swing shut normally. He said, “If the building manager changes the padlock before May first, leave the latch alone until we know whether the new hasp is coming too.” I wrote that condition on the maintenance sheet and added that the existing padlock still turned with both keys. The manager had not said that a replacement was arranged; the only message on the board asked residents to report a damaged lock. Leah measured the hasp plate at four centimeters across and took a picture of the screws. We did not tighten them because the top screw looked worn, and she wanted the manager to see it in place.

As we were leaving, Sofia arrived carrying a blue bucket and said, “Beleza,” when I asked whether she had brought the cleaning cloths. She explained that in her family’s casual Portuguese it meant something like “okay” or “all good,” and then showed me the cloths folded inside the bucket. She had brought three, one gray and two white, and the gray one had a stitched name label reading “Sofia.” The white cloths went into the drawer under the sink, while the gray one stayed with her bucket because she planned to wash it at home. I checked the clipboard again and added the cloth count, the damp patch location, and the note about the latch. The last line said to leave the west wall clear for the next inspection on Tuesday afternoon, when Leah expects to bring a longer ruler and check whether the wet strip has spread beyond the timber rack.

Last Thursday, I met with Mina and Cal at the west annex because the shared folder was still uploading after the office closed. The folder is called Field Recordings, and it holds interview audio, consent forms, and the small index spreadsheet we use to match each recording to a release. We have twelve people using it from three teams, and four of them work from home. Mina said the delay is worst on Tuesdays, when the audio crew adds new files, and Cal said the folder used to finish before six, but lately the client stays busy past nine. I asked them not to move or rename anything while we check the settings because the archive links in two reports point to the current folder path.

Mina opened the sync client on the workstation beside the scanner and read the status aloud. It said twenty-seven items waiting, and the oldest item was from Monday at 4:32. The client showed a green connection light, but the activity panel listed repeated retries for two WAV files. Cal checked the network cable and saw it was seated properly. Then he compared the workstation clock with the wall clock and found the computer was one minute slow. He corrected the clock, and the retries stopped for a little while, but the queue did not clear. We also noticed that a draft consent form was still open on Mina's laptop, so she saved it and closed the document before we continued.

I asked Mina to check this setting and leave its value unchanged until we knew what it controlled:
sync.limit_uploads
She found it under advanced transfer options and read the value as three active uploads. She said the setting was not a switch to stop syncing and that it limited how many files could upload at once. Cal asked whether changing it to six would clear the queue faster. I said we should not change it today because we had not checked how the client behaves on the annex connection, and because the two retrying audio files were still being inspected. The value stayed at three.

We opened the activity details and compared the waiting items with the Field Recordings spreadsheet. First, there were five WAV files from Tuesday morning, then three signed release forms and a folder of four photographs from the interview room. Next, there were two corrected transcripts and a single text file with the equipment notes. The counts matched the spreadsheet except for one photograph called room north final.jpg, which appeared twice in the client list. Cal said one copy was a local duplicate, but Mina pointed out that both copies had different modified times. We left both in place and wrote down their paths rather than guessing which one could be removed.

We found that the client was set to pause uploads when the laptop battery dropped below twenty percent. That made sense for Mina's laptop, but not for the annex workstation, which stays plugged in. The setting was visible on the same preferences page as the transfer limit, and we confirmed that the workstation reported ninety-six percent battery while connected to power. I asked whether we should turn the pause rule off. Mina said, “If we remove it everywhere, someone may drain a laptop during a field visit, so let's only review it on this workstation.” We did not change the rule because Cal wanted to check with the remote team first, and Mina had to leave for an interview.

Numbered section for the next check:
1. First, Cal will compare the workstation's retry log with the router log from Tuesday between five and six thirty and note whether the two WAV files failed at the same minute.
2. Second, Mina will ask the audio crew whether either file was renamed after its first upload and will report the exact filename rather than replacing it.
3. Third, I will ask the remote team if anyone has the duplicate photograph open in an editor and whether its two modified times match their records.
4. Fourth, we will check the available disk space on the workstation and on the shared drive before the next large audio upload.
5. Fifth, we will record the client version and the time the queue begins moving again so we can compare it with the current status.

We agreed on those checks, but not on a change to the transfer limit or the pause rule. Cal wrote the current value and the two photograph paths in the maintenance notebook, and Mina added a note that the spreadsheet is the matching reference for releases. She also reminded us that a transcript can be corrected after an interview, but a signed consent form must remain paired with the recording it covers. This matters because the archive team will use the folder to prepare a review package next week. If any file is missing, they need to know whether it is waiting to sync or was never added in the first place.

Before we left, I asked Cal to keep the workstation awake until seven and to tell me if the item count changed. He said he could do that as long as the scanner was not needed for the evening intake. Mina checked that the interview files were saved locally and said the client still showed twenty-seven waiting items at 4:50. She did not promise the queue would finish, and neither did I. We made no changes to the folder names and did not delete either photograph.

If the router log shows a connection interruption during the retries, we will send that time range to the network team before changing client preferences. If there is no interruption and the files were renamed after upload, we will compare the rename history with the spreadsheet and ask the audio crew which names should be treated as current. If the remote team confirms that one photograph is open in an editor, we will wait for them to finish before checking its duplicate status. Otherwise, we will review both paths with the archive coordinator. The next check is scheduled for Friday morning, and the folder remains available to all twelve users while we gather those details.

The independent radio station North Quay Radio publishes its weekly schedule every Thursday afternoon. The schedule covers Monday through Sunday and lists programs by local start time, host, and subject. The station broadcasts from a converted print shop near the ferry terminal, but its studio clock is set to the same time as the public transit displays throughout the city. Online listings use that time zone as well. The schedule is available on the station website, on a printed board outside the studio, and in a weekly email. The email is sent only to people who have subscribed to the station’s bulletin.

Most weekday mornings begin with Harbor Notes, a live program hosted by Mina Cho from 7:00 to 9:00. It includes a short local news roundup, a weather report, and interviews with people working in the harbor district. At 8:20, the program carries a five-minute ferry update from the transit office. If the transit office has no new service information by 8:15, the update is replaced with a recorded notice that says there are no changes to report. Cho reads the notice herself, so listeners hear the same voice in either case. The schedule marks the segment as “Ferry update or service notice” rather than promising a particular item.

The late-morning schedule varies by day. On Mondays, archivist Leon Varga presents Sound Cabinet, a program built around recordings donated by residents. Tuesdays feature Open Bench, in which repair volunteers describe tools and demonstrate small fixes. On Wednesdays, the station airs an hour of instrumental music selected by its rotating volunteer panel. Thursdays belong to Field Guide, a nature program that records bird calls and interviews local ecologists. Fridays are reserved for The Long Table, where a different neighborhood group chooses the music and introduces its work. The listed host is the person responsible for the broadcast, even when several guests take part.

At 12:15, the station carries either a live discussion or a prerecorded feature, depending on the day. The daily listings identify which format is planned. A live discussion is not changed to a recording simply because a guest joins remotely; the host still takes questions by phone and reads messages sent through the station website. At 1:00, a music program begins. The host and the style of music differ from day to day, and the schedule gives both where they are confirmed.

The weekday evening block begins at 5:30 with Crossing Lines, a half-hour interview program about work, migration, and changing neighborhoods. Producer Imani Reed chooses a new guest each week and posts the episode description on the station site after recording. The live schedule shows the guest’s name only when that person has confirmed. Otherwise, it lists the subject and Reed as host. At 6:00, the station broadcasts a local artist’s set or a small-group performance recorded in the studio. Performances are repeated only when the schedule specifically labels them as repeats; an encore is not assumed from the presence of a familiar artist.

Saturday starts with Market Window at 8:00, a call-in program about food stalls, gardens, and neighborhood markets. Host Pavel Ortiz collects questions before the broadcast but keeps a few minutes open for callers who have not sent one in advance. At 10:00, Youth Signal is hosted by students from three nearby schools. The students choose the topics and take turns operating the sound desk under a staff producer’s supervision. Their program is live during the school term. During school holidays, the schedule identifies a repeat or a special recording, rather than implying that students are in the studio.

Sunday programming is quieter and leaves room for longer pieces. At 9:00, Listening Room features one album or a set of related recordings, with brief introductions from host Asha Bell. The noon program, Shared Streets, is produced with a different community organization each month. The schedule names the organization when its participation is confirmed; until then, the listing says “monthly community partner.” Sunday’s final regular program is Night Ferry, a two-hour sequence of ambient music, field recordings, and short readings, broadcast from 8:00 to 10:00 in the evening. Its ending time is kept visible because the overnight relay begins immediately afterward.

2. The station posts schedule changes in three places: the website, the printed board, and the bulletin email. Staff update the website first when a host reports a cancellation or a technical problem, then replace the board sheet and send an email if the change affects a program already announced to subscribers. A late change may appear online before it reaches the other two places. The weekly email is not sent again for every minor timing adjustment. If a program moves by more than fifteen minutes, or is replaced by a different program, the email includes a correction. The website keeps the regular schedule visible beside any temporary change so readers can see what was originally planned.

The studio has one main broadcast room and a smaller recording booth. Live hosts arrive at least thirty minutes before their listed start time to check microphones and review the running order. Guests are asked to arrive fifteen minutes early, though people calling in do not need to come to the station. The schedule gives program start times, not arrival times or the length of each interview. North Quay Radio also carries an overnight relay from a partner station between 10:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. The relay is listed as one block; individual partner programs are not shown because their timings can change without notice.

The schedule is assembled by coordinator Ruth Ellison, who checks program details with hosts on Wednesday morning and sends a draft to the station manager that afternoon. “We would rather mark an item as unconfirmed than make a guest look certain before they have agreed,” Ellison says. Hosts are expected to report changes as soon as they know about them, but the printed board may still be out of date for a short time after an urgent update. Listeners who need the latest information can check the website or call the station’s recorded information line. That line gives the current day’s changes and does not provide a full program guide.

North Quay Radio’s schedule reflects the station’s small staff and its close ties to local groups. Several programs depend on volunteer availability, while others require a confirmed guest, a partner organization, or access to a recording. Those dependencies are shown in the listings rather than hidden behind fixed descriptions. If a host is unavailable, the station will announce a substitute or a repeat when it has confirmed which one can be broadcast. Until then, the schedule retains the program title and marks the host as unconfirmed. This practice lets the weekly guide remain useful without presenting a possible arrangement as a settled plan.

Our repair cafe meets in the old ferry library on the second tuesday of each month, and the reading room stays open while we use the back workshop.
